rv.q: Olivier’s – to judge by the 1960 film – is the superior performance, blessed with a mercurial vitality and dangerous mischief that the benign Branagh can’t match. Yet Sir Ken goes some considerable and impressive way to stamping his own authority and personality on the part.
While it’s a highly watchable performance, it deserves a better production.
That level of suffocation is never achieved in the Branagh Company production which opened in the West End last night.
When Osborne is at his most vicious, The Entertainer flares into life: male despair and venom writ large.
What a pity you spend stretches of this revival longing for more than the snifter of throttled rage and raddled ennui that Rob Ashford’s production provides.

Branagh opts for a knowing, oily and energised Archie rather than the “dead behind the eyes”, audience-hating, cynical avoider of the British tax man, he claims to be; He also looked 15 years too young for the part.
Yet somehow, in Rob Ashford’s heavy-handed production, the play and the performance fail to ignite.

cn.t: Branagh steps into Olivier's iconic shoes as fading music-hall comic Archie Rice, but critics find the production misjudged and unconvincing, failing to capture the throttled rage of Osborne's post-Suez portrait of British decline.
